title: Bitte buchstabieren Sie

situation.setting: At the course office, Raj has to give his name and phone number for the registration form.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber
lines.en: Thank you. And the phone number?

lines.speaker: Raj
lines.de: Null, eins, sieben, sechs, vier, fünf, acht, neun, zwei, drei.
lines.en: Zero, one, seven, six, four, five, eight, nine, two, three.

grammar.title: Numbers 0–10 and the alphabet
grammar.intro: You need two things to give personal details: the numbers and the letter names. Learn the letter names by ear: in German you spell names aloud all the time, on the phone and at the desk.

examples.de: Ich heiße Patel: P – A – T – E – L.
examples.en: My name is Patel: P – A – T – E – L.

watchOut: ei sounds like English “eye” (zwei, drei) and eu sounds like “oy” (neun). ie is a long “ee” (sieben, vier).
On the phone zwei is often said zwo, so it isn't confused with drei.
bitte means both “please” and “you're welcome”. Use it when you ask for something and when someone thanks you.

exercises.prompt: You didn't catch someone's name. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Entschuldigung is “excuse me”, handy for getting someone's attention or asking them to repeat.
A polite request to Sie puts the verb before Sie.

exercises.prompt: Someone says “Danke!” to you. How do you reply?

culture: Germans often ask you to spell your name, so practise it. Phone numbers are usually said in pairs or in short groups of digits, and Germans write the date as day.month.year. Say Entschuldigung to get attention politely, for example in a shop or on the bus.
canDo: I can spell my name aloud.
I can say bitte, danke and Entschuldigung at the right moment.
